lesson_text: What he loses if the stop gets hit. On $100,000, 1% is $1,000. That's the money he's agreed to give up if he's wrong, measured against the whole account. It's not how much he bought. He can have a lot more than that in the stock, and the stop decides how much of it is really on the line. Thinking this way puts every trade on the same scale. A 1% loss is a 1% loss, whatever the stock or the price. Risk is what you lose at the stop, measured against the whole account.

lesson_text: Account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop. The stop is in the math on purpose. Entry minus stop is what each share loses if you're wrong. Divide your dollars at risk by it and you get the shares that lose exactly your plan. Risk $500 with a $20 stop distance and you buy 25 shares. Round down, never up. Then check it against the 40% cap and take the smaller one. If the honest stop is too far away for your risk, you pass. You don't squeeze the stop to make it fit. Stop first, then the math. Dollars at risk over the stop distance, round down, then check the cap.

wrong.Recalculate only at year end: Too seldom. Weekly or monthly, so your number is never months out of date.

lesson_text: All 400 at one price, with one stop. That's how we do it: full size on the trigger, no starter, and no plan to add later. The 400 already came from your stop and the cap, so it's the right risk. Split it and only half your size gets the best entry you'll see. The add comes higher with the same stop, so those shares carry more risk each. If 400 feels like too much, that's telling you something. Buy fewer from the start, or pass. steps: Before the open, write the entry, stop and size for every buy. Then a focus list of the 5 to 10 best.
In the session, it's market orders, regular hours only. And a real stop with your broker, not one in your head.
No new buys in the 3 days before earnings. Hold through one only if you're up 5R.

sources.name: Our trading rules
sources.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens. ("39 yes") … Each day, a focus list of the 5 to 10 best setups; the rest are ignored. ("64 yes.") … Entries are market orders. ("57, No i market order everything.") The stop still sits with the broker (D41). … No new buys outside regular trading hours. ("58, that is fine.") … Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. ("41, yes.") … No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. ("22 change it to 3 days and only hold if up 5R.") … Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. … Journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally. ("27, ideally yes..")
